notes:
1. Meaning of Union Executive

  • The Union Executive is the executive branch of the Government of India.
  • It forms the administrative backbone of national governance.

Its major responsibilities include:

  • Implementing laws.
  • Administering the country.
  • Formulating public policy.
  • Maintaining internal administration.
  • Conducting foreign affairs.
  • Defending the nation.
  • The Union Executive functions according to the Constitution and remains accountable to Parliament.
📌 Must-Memorise

Union Executive → Part V → Chapter I → Articles 52–78

2. Constitutional Framework

The Union Executive is dealt with in:

  • Part V — The Union.
  • Chapter I — The Executive.
  • Articles 52–78.
  • India follows a Parliamentary or Cabinet system of government.
  • The President is the constitutional head.
  • The Prime Minister and Council of Ministers exercise actual political executive authority.

3. Components of the Union Executive

The attached notes identify the principal Union Executive offices as:

  • President.
  • Vice-President.
  • Prime Minister.
  • Council of Ministers.
  • Attorney General of India.
📌 Must-Memorise

President → Constitutional Head

Prime Minister → Head of Government

Council of Ministers → Real Collective Executive

Attorney General → Highest Law Officer

4. Nominal and Real Executive

President:

  • Constitutional head.
  • Nominal or de jure executive.
  • Executive power formally vested under Article 53.

Prime Minister and Council of Ministers:

  • Real or de facto executive.
  • Exercise actual executive authority.
  • Politically responsible to Lok Sabha.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Article 53 → Power Vested in President

Article 74 → Power Exercised on Ministerial Aid and Advice

5. Parliamentary Executive

Important characteristics include:

  • Executive drawn from Legislature.
  • Council of Ministers collectively responsible to Lok Sabha.
  • Prime Minister heads Government.
  • President acts on ministerial advice.
  • Executive remains in office while it enjoys Lok Sabha confidence.
  • Legislature and Executive are closely coordinated.

6. Collective Responsibility

  • The Council of Ministers remains in office only while it enjoys the confidence of the Lok Sabha.
  • If it loses majority support, the Council must resign.
  • Collective responsibility provides democratic accountability of the Executive to the House of the People.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 75(3) → Collective Responsibility to Lok Sabha

7. Fields of Executive Action

Union Executive functions extend to:

  • Administration.
  • Legislation.
  • Finance.
  • Defence.
  • Foreign affairs.
  • Appointments.
  • Emergencies.
  • Diplomacy.
  • National governance.
  • Many constitutional acts are formally performed in the President's name but practically carried out on ministerial advice.

8. Constitutional Article Map

  • Article 52 → President.
  • Article 53 → Union executive power.
  • Articles 54–62 → Election, term and related provisions of President.
  • Articles 63–71 → Vice-President.
  • Article 72 → Pardoning power.
  • Article 73 → Extent of Union executive power.
  • Article 74 → Aid and advice.
  • Article 75 → Ministers.
  • Article 76 → Attorney General.
  • Article 77 → Government business.
  • Article 78 → Prime Minister's duties.

9. President — Constitutional Position

  • Article 52 provides that there shall be a President of India.
  • Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the President.
  • Article 74 requires the President ordinarily to exercise constitutional power on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.

The President is:

  • Head of State.
  • Constitutional head.
  • Nominal or de jure executive.
  • The Prime Minister is the political head of Government.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 52 → President

Article 53 → Executive Power

Article 74 → Aid and Advice

10. Constitutional Neutrality of the President

The President is expected to:

  • Remain above party politics.
  • Act according to the Constitution.
  • Serve the national interest.
  • Follow constitutional principles.
  • The office symbolises continuity and constitutional governance rather than partisan political authority.

11. President as Symbol of National Unity

The office represents:

  • Unity of India.
  • Continuity of Government.
  • Constitutional governance.
  • Sovereignty of the Republic.
  • National constitutional authority.

12. Formal Constitutional Acts of the President

The President formally performs functions such as:

  • Appointing Prime Minister.
  • Appointing Governors.
  • Appointing judges and constitutional authorities.
  • Promulgating Ordinances.
  • Granting or withholding assent to Bills.
  • Issuing Emergency proclamations.
  • Appointing Ambassadors.
  • Concluding treaties in India's name subject to constitutional procedures.
  • Most such functions are exercised on ministerial advice.

13. Presidential Oath

The President takes an oath to:

  • Faithfully execute the office.
  • Preserve, protect and defend the Constitution.
  • Preserve the law.
  • Devote the office to the service and well-being of the people.
  • The oath is administered by the Chief Justice of India.
  • In the Chief Justice's absence, it is administered by the senior-most available Supreme Court judge.
📌 Must-Memorise

President's Oath → Chief Justice of India

14. Office and Residence of the President

  • Salary and allowances are determined by Parliament.
  • Official residence is Rashtrapati Bhavan, New Delhi.
  • Presidential emoluments cannot ordinarily be reduced during the term, subject to the constitutional Financial Emergency framework.

15. Constitutional Immunities of the President

During the term of office:

  • President is not answerable to a court for exercise of official powers and duties.
  • No criminal proceeding may be instituted or continued against the President.
  • President cannot be arrested or imprisoned.
  • Personal civil proceedings require prescribed prior notice.
  • These protections safeguard the dignity and independence of the office.
  • They do not place the President above the Constitution.

16. Article 54 — Presidential Election

  • The President is indirectly elected.
  • Election occurs through a constitutionally constituted Electoral College.

The electoral system gives representation to both:

  • Parliament.
  • States.
  • It therefore combines parliamentary and federal principles.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 54 → Presidential Electoral College

17. Members Included in Presidential Electoral College

Included:

  • Elected members of Lok Sabha.
  • Elected members of Rajya Sabha.
  • Elected members of Legislative Assemblies of all States.
  • Elected members of Legislative Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry.

18. Members Excluded from Presidential Electoral College

Excluded:

  • Nominated Members of Parliament.
  • Nominated State Assembly members, if any.
  • Members of State Legislative Councils.
  • Nominated members of Delhi and Puducherry Assemblies.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

President Election → Elected MPs + Elected MLAs

MLCs → Excluded

Nominated MPs → Excluded

19. Why the President Is Indirectly Elected

Reasons identified in the notes include:

  • India follows parliamentary government.
  • President is constitutional rather than real executive.
  • Direct election could create rivalry with Prime Minister.
  • Indirect election is practical for a large democracy.
  • Participation of States preserves federal character.

20. Article 55 — Federal Balance

Article 55 seeks:

  • Uniformity among States.
  • Parity between Union and States.
  • Weighted voting is therefore used.
  • Every MLA does not have the same vote value.
  • Every MP's vote also carries a calculated value.

21. Value of an MLA's Vote

Formula:

Population of State ÷ (Total elected MLAs × 1000)

  • If the remainder is 500 or more, one is added to the quotient.
  • The population basis presently uses the 1971 Census under the constitutional freeze described in the attached notes.
📌 Must-Memorise

MLA Vote → State Population ÷ Elected MLAs × 1000

22. Value of an MP's Vote

Formula:

Total value of votes of all elected MLAs ÷ Total elected MPs

  • This creates approximate parity between Parliament and State Legislative Assemblies.

23. Method of Presidential Election

The election uses:

  • Proportional Representation.
  • Single Transferable Vote.
  • Secret ballot.
  • Preferential voting.

Electors may mark:

  • First preference.
  • Second preference.
  • Third preference.
  • Further preferences.
📌 Must-Memorise

President Election → PR + STV + Secret Ballot

24. Counting and Quota

  • A candidate must secure the prescribed quota of valid vote value.

If no candidate reaches the quota initially:

  • Candidate with the lowest first-preference total is eliminated.
  • Votes are transferred according to next available preferences.
  • The process continues until a candidate reaches the required quota.

25. Vacancies in Electoral College

  • A Presidential election is not invalid merely because of vacancies in the Electoral College.

Vacancies may arise from:

  • Death.
  • Resignation.
  • Disqualification.
  • Dissolution of a House.
  • This is subject to constitutional provisions.

26. Presidential Election Disputes

  • All disputes relating to Presidential election are decided exclusively by the Supreme Court.

Constitutional basis:

  • Article 71.
  • Supreme Court's decision is final and binding.
📌 Must-Memorise

President Election Dispute → Supreme Court → Article 71

27. Qualifications under Article 58

A candidate for President must:

  • Be a citizen of India.
  • Have completed 35 years of age.
  • Be qualified for election to Lok Sabha.

Not hold an office of profit under:

  • Union.
  • State.
  • Local authority.
  • Government-controlled authority.

28. Offices Not Treated as Office of Profit

For Presidential qualification, offices such as the following are not treated as disqualifying offices of profit:

  • President.
  • Vice-President.
  • Governor.
  • Union Minister.
  • State Minister.

29. Presidential Nomination Requirements

Nomination requires:

  • At least 50 electors as proposers.
  • At least 50 electors as seconders.
  • Prescribed security deposit under election law.
📌 Must-Memorise

President Nomination → 50 Proposers + 50 Seconders

30. Presidential Term

  • Normal term → Five years from entering office.
  • President continues beyond the term until successor assumes office.
  • Re-election is permitted any number of times.
📌 Must-Memorise

President → 5 Years

Re-election → No Constitutional Limit Mentioned in Notes

31. Presidential Resignation

  • President resigns by addressing resignation to the Vice-President.
  • The Vice-President communicates the resignation to the Speaker of Lok Sabha.
📌 Must-Memorise

President Resignation → Vice-President

32. Conditions of Presidential Office

  • President cannot remain a member of Parliament.
  • President cannot remain a member of a State Legislature.
  • If a legislator is elected President, the legislative seat becomes vacant upon entering Presidential office.

33. Vacancy in Presidential Office

A vacancy may arise due to:

  • Expiry of term.
  • Resignation.
  • Impeachment.
  • Death.
  • Disqualification.
  • Inability to discharge functions.
  • Election being declared void.
  • Other constitutional cause.

34. Ground for Impeachment

The only constitutional ground for impeachment is:

  • Violation of the Constitution.
  • The expression is not defined in the Constitution according to the attached notes.
  • No President of India has been impeached so far in the source material.
📌 Must-Memorise

President Impeachment → Violation of Constitution

35. Article 61 — Initiation of Impeachment

  • Either House of Parliament may initiate impeachment.
  • The charge must be in writing.
  • At least one-fourth of the total membership of the initiating House must sign the notice.
  • At least 14 days' written notice must be given to the President.
📌 Must-Memorise

Impeachment Notice → 1/4 Members + 14 Days

36. Voting for Impeachment

The initiating House must pass the resolution by not less than:

  • Two-thirds of its total membership.
  • The other House then investigates the charge.

President has a right to:

  • Appear personally.
  • Be represented through counsel.

The investigating House must also pass the resolution by:

  • Two-thirds of its total membership.
  • Removal takes effect on that date.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Impeachment Majority → 2/3 of Total Membership in Both Houses

37. Key Features of Impeachment

  • Only Parliament can impeach.
  • Either House may initiate.
  • Only ground is violation of Constitution.
  • Special majority required in both Houses.
  • President has right of defence.
  • No court conducts impeachment.

38. Article 62 — Election to Fill Vacancy

If vacancy arises by expiry:

  • Election should be completed before expiration of existing term.

If casual vacancy arises:

  • Election must be held within six months.

The newly elected President receives:

  • Full five-year term.
  • Not merely the remainder of predecessor's term.
📌 Must-Memorise

Casual Vacancy → Election within 6 Months → New Full 5-Year Term

39. Acting President

If Presidential office becomes vacant:

  • Vice-President acts as President.

If both President and Vice-President are unavailable:

  • Chief Justice of India acts.

If Chief Justice is unavailable:

  • Senior-most available Supreme Court judge performs the functions.

40. Categories of Presidential Powers

Presidential powers may be classified as:

  • Executive.
  • Legislative.
  • Financial.
  • Judicial.
  • Diplomatic.
  • Military.
  • Emergency.

41. Executive Appointments

The President formally appoints authorities including:

  • Prime Minister.
  • Union Ministers.
  • Governors.
  • Attorney General.
  • CAG.
  • Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners.
  • UPSC Chairperson and members.
  • Finance Commission members.
  • Supreme Court judges.
  • High Court judges.
  • Ambassadors.
  • High Commissioners.
  • Other constitutional authorities as provided by law.
  • Appointments follow relevant constitutional advice and procedure.

42. Administrative Functions

  • Union executive actions are taken in the President's name.

Rules govern:

  • Allocation of Government business.
  • Transaction of Government business.
  • President receives reports from constitutional authorities.
  • Union Territories are administered through appointed administrators where applicable.

43. Legislative Functions

The President:

  • Is an integral part of Parliament.
  • Summons Parliament.
  • Prorogues Parliament.
  • Dissolves Lok Sabha.
  • Addresses Parliament.
  • Sends messages to Parliament.
  • Nominates members where constitutionally provided.
  • Assents to Bills.
  • Returns eligible Bills.
  • Promulgates Ordinances under Article 123.

44. Financial Functions

The President:

  • Gives previous recommendation for introduction of a Money Bill.
  • Causes the Union Budget to be laid before Parliament.
  • Recommends demands involving the Consolidated Fund.
  • Constitutes the Finance Commission every five years.

45. Judicial Functions

Under Article 72, the President may exercise powers of:

  • Pardon.
  • Reprieve.
  • Respite.
  • Remission.
  • Suspension.
  • Commutation.

46. Diplomatic Functions

The President formally:

  • Represents India internationally.
  • Appoints diplomats.
  • Receives foreign diplomats.
  • Concludes treaties in India's name subject to constitutional requirements.

47. Military Functions

  • President is the Supreme Commander of the Defence Forces.

President formally appoints the chiefs of:

  • Army.
  • Navy.
  • Air Force.
  • War and peace remain subject to parliamentary and constitutional control.

48. Emergency Powers

Presidential Emergency powers include:

  • Article 352 → National Emergency.
  • Article 356 → President's Rule.
  • Article 360 → Financial Emergency.
  • These powers operate on ministerial advice and subject to constitutional safeguards.

49. Article 123 — Ordinance Power

  • Article 123 gives the President temporary legislative power where Parliament cannot enact a law immediately.
  • It is an exceptional power intended for urgent circumstances.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 123 → Presidential Ordinance

50. Conditions for Ordinance

An Ordinance may be issued when:

  • Both Houses are not in session, or
  • One House is not in session, and
  • Parliament is therefore unable to legislate, and
  • Circumstances require immediate action.

51. Aid and Advice for Ordinance

  • Presidential satisfaction under Article 123 operates on aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.
  • Ordinance power is not ordinarily exercised independently by the President.

52. Legal Force of Ordinance

  • An Ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament during its valid operation.
  • It remains temporary.
  • Parliament retains primary legislative authority.

53. Duration of Ordinance

  • Ordinance ceases six weeks after Parliament reassembles unless approved.

If Houses reassemble on different dates:

  • Six weeks are counted from the later date.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ordinance → 6 Weeks from Reassembly of Parliament

54. Parliament's Options on Ordinance

Parliament may:

  • Approve it and replace it with an Act.
  • Replace it with a different law.
  • Modify its provisions through legislation.
  • Allow it to lapse.

55. Withdrawal of Ordinance

  • The President may withdraw an Ordinance before expiry.
  • This ordinarily occurs on advice of the Council of Ministers.

56. Legislative Competence of Ordinance

An Ordinance may deal with:

  • Union List subjects.
  • Concurrent List subjects.
  • Other fields where Parliament is constitutionally competent.

It cannot deal with:

  • Matters outside Parliament's legislative competence.

57. Constitutional Limits on Ordinances

An Ordinance:

  • Cannot violate Fundamental Rights.
  • Cannot alter Basic Structure.
  • Must remain within legislative competence.
  • Is subject to judicial review.

58. D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar, 1987

  • Routine re-promulgation of Ordinances was held constitutionally impermissible.
  • Ordinance power is an emergency mechanism.
  • It cannot become a substitute for Legislature.
📌 Must-Memorise

D.C. Wadhwa → 1987 → Re-promulgation Unconstitutional

59. Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar, 2017

  • Ordinances are subject to judicial review.
  • Repeated re-promulgation cannot be used to bypass Legislature.
  • Constitutional conditions governing Ordinance power must be respected.
📌 Must-Memorise

Krishna Kumar Singh → 2017 → Ordinance Judicial Review

60. Article 111 — Presidential Assent

Presidential assent produces commonly described veto forms:

  • Absolute Veto.
  • Suspensive Veto.
  • Pocket Veto.
  • The Constitution itself does not use the word “veto.”

61. Absolute Veto

  • President withholds assent.
  • Bill ends.

The notes associate it generally with situations such as:

  • Private Member's Bill.
  • Government Bill where ministry resigns and succeeding Government advises against assent.

62. Suspensive Veto

  • President returns an Ordinary Bill for reconsideration.

Parliament may pass it again:

  • With amendments.
  • Without amendments.
  • If repassed, Presidential assent becomes mandatory.
  • A Money Bill cannot be returned in this manner.
📌 Must-Memorise

Suspensive Veto → Ordinary Bill Only

Repassed Bill → Assent Mandatory

63. Pocket Veto

  • President takes no action on the Bill.
  • Bill remains pending.
  • The Constitution provides no general time limit for Presidential action on an Ordinary Bill.

Famous example in the notes:

  • President Giani Zail Singh.
  • Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986.
📌 Must-Memorise

Pocket Veto Example → Giani Zail Singh → 1986 Post Office Bill

64. Qualified Veto

  • India does not have a Qualified Veto.
  • Unlike the United States, there is no special legislative-majority override mechanism of that type in the Indian constitutional system described in the notes.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Qualified Veto → Not Available in India

65. Constitutional Amendment Bills

  • President must assent to a duly passed Constitutional Amendment Bill under Article 368.

President:

  • Cannot return it.
  • Cannot withhold assent.
📌 Must-Memorise

Constitution Amendment Bill → Presidential Assent Mandatory

66. State Bills Reserved for President

  • Certain State Bills may be reserved by Governor for consideration of the President.
  • Their detailed treatment belongs to the State Executive chapter.

67. Article 72 — Pardoning Power

  • Article 72 provides the President's constitutional clemency power.
  • It allows exceptional relief where justice may require mercy.
  • It is not an ordinary appeal from a judicial decision.

68. Cases Covered by Article 72

President's pardoning power covers:

  • Court-martial cases.
  • Offences within Union executive power.
  • All death-sentence cases.
📌 Must-Memorise

President → Court Martial + Union Matters + Death Sentence

69. Forms of Clemency

Pardon:

  • Completely removes conviction, sentence, punishment and resulting disqualifications.

Commutation:

  • Substitutes a lighter form of punishment.

Remission:

  • Reduces duration without changing the character of punishment.

Respite:

  • Awards a lesser sentence due to special circumstances.

Reprieve:

  • Temporarily postpones execution.

Suspension:

  • Temporarily suspends operation of sentence.

70. Clemency Examples

  • Death sentence → Life imprisonment → Commutation.
  • Ten years → Six years with same form of punishment → Remission.
  • Lesser sentence due to pregnancy, disability, age or serious illness → Respite.
  • Temporary delay to permit mercy proceedings → Reprieve.

71. President vs Governor — Clemency

President under Article 72:

  • Court-martial cases.
  • May pardon death sentence.
  • Union executive matters.

Governor under Article 161:

  • No court-martial pardon.
  • Cannot pardon death sentence according to the attached notes, though may suspend, remit or commute where constitutionally applicable.
  • State executive matters.

72. Aid and Advice in Clemency

  • Article 72 is exercised on aid and advice of Council of Ministers.
  • It is a constitutional power rather than a personal Presidential power.

73. Judicial Review of Clemency

Courts may review mercy decisions on limited grounds such as:

  • Mala fides.
  • Arbitrariness.
  • Irrelevant considerations.
  • Non-application of mind.
  • Constitutional impropriety.
  • Courts do not simply substitute their own view on whether mercy should have been granted.

74. Maru Ram v. Union of India, 1980

  • Clemency power is exercised on Cabinet advice.
  • It is a constitutional power and not a personal Presidential discretion.
📌 Must-Memorise

Maru Ram → 1980 → Clemency on Cabinet Advice

75. Kehar Singh v. Union of India, 1989

  • President may broadly examine the merits of a mercy petition.
  • Exercise remains subject to constitutional limits.

76. Epuru Sudhakar v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, 2006

Clemency decisions may be reviewed if:

  • Mala fide.
  • Arbitrary.
  • Based on irrelevant considerations.

77. Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India, 2014

  • Unreasonable delay in mercy proceedings may become relevant in death-sentence relief.
  • Human dignity remains constitutionally significant.

78. Presidential Discretion — General Rule

  • Presidential discretion is exceptional.
  • The ordinary rule is aid and advice under Article 74.
  • President cannot independently govern or formulate Government policy.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

President → Limited Constitutional Discretion

Ministerial Advice → General Rule

79. Appointment of Prime Minister in Hung Lok Sabha

  • If no party has a clear majority, President may invite the person most likely to command Lok Sabha confidence.
  • Majority must ultimately be demonstrated through the House.

80. Loss of Majority

  • Where majority support is doubtful, a floor test may be required.
  • Majority should be established in Lok Sabha rather than decided at Rashtrapati Bhavan.

81. Sudden Vacancy in Prime Ministership

  • If Prime Minister dies or resigns without an immediate successor, President may appoint an interim Prime Minister until governing party or coalition selects a leader.

82. Reconsideration of Ministerial Advice

  • The 44th Amendment permits President to return ministerial advice once for reconsideration.

If Council of Ministers reiterates the advice:

  • President is bound to accept it.
📌 Must-Memorise

President → Can Return Advice Once

Reiterated Advice → Binding

83. Article 78 and Presidential Information

President may require information relating to:

  • Union administration.
  • Legislative proposals.
  • Matters decided by an individual Minister.
  • President may ask Prime Minister to place an individual Minister's decision before the full Council.

84. Limits on Presidential Independence

President cannot:

  • Formulate policy independently.
  • Permanently reject Cabinet decisions.
  • Govern without a Council of Ministers.
  • Exercise power contrary to binding constitutional advice.

85. Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab, 1955

  • India follows a parliamentary executive.
  • Real executive authority is exercised by Council of Ministers.
  • Executive power broadly follows legislative competence, subject to Constitution.

86. Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab, 1974

  • President and Governors are constitutional heads.
  • They ordinarily act on ministerial advice.
  • Personal discretion is limited.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shamsher Singh → 1974 → Constitutional Head + Limited Discretion

87. S.R. Bommai v. Union of India, 1994

  • Majority should ordinarily be tested on the floor of the House.
  • Subjective executive assessment should not replace the legislative floor test.
📌 Must-Memorise

S.R. Bommai → Floor Test

88. Vice-President — Constitutional Basis

  • Article 63 → There shall be a Vice-President.
  • Article 64 → Ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha.
  • Article 65 → Acts as President.
  • Articles 66–71 → Election, term, oath, vacancy and disputes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vice-President → Articles 63–71

89. Two Roles of Vice-President

The Vice-President performs two major constitutional roles:

  • Vice-President of India.
  • Ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha.
  • The attached notes clarify that the office does not operate as part of the Union Executive in exactly the same manner as the President, but performs important succession and parliamentary functions.

90. Vice-Presidential Electoral College

Included:

  • Elected Lok Sabha members.
  • Elected Rajya Sabha members.
  • Nominated Rajya Sabha members.
  • Nominated Lok Sabha members where constitutionally present.

Excluded:

  • State MLAs.
  • State MLCs.
  • Non-parliamentary electoral bodies.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

President Election → MPs + State MLAs

Vice-President Election → MPs Only

91. Vice-Presidential Election Method

Election is:

  • Indirect.
  • Proportional Representation.
  • Single Transferable Vote.
  • Secret ballot.

92. Vice-Presidential Qualifications

Candidate must:

  • Be a citizen of India.
  • Have completed 35 years.
  • Be qualified for election to Rajya Sabha.
  • Not hold an office of profit under Government.
📌 Must-Memorise

President → Qualified for Lok Sabha

Vice-President → Qualified for Rajya Sabha

93. Vice-President's Oath and Term

  • Oath is administered by President.
  • Vice-President swears allegiance to Constitution and faithful discharge of duties.
  • Term → Five years.
  • Continues until successor assumes office.

94. Vice-Presidential Resignation and Removal

  • Resignation is addressed to President.
  • Vice-President is not impeached.

Removal:

  • Initiated in Rajya Sabha.
  • Requires majority of all then members of Rajya Sabha.
  • Lok Sabha must agree by simple majority.
  • At least 14 days' notice is required.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

President → Impeachment

Vice-President → Removal Resolution, Not Impeachment

95. Vice-President as Chairman of Rajya Sabha

The Vice-President:

  • Presides over Rajya Sabha.
  • Maintains order.
  • Interprets procedural rules.
  • Conducts debates.
  • Decides points of order.
  • Is not a member of Rajya Sabha.
  • Has no ordinary first-instance vote.
  • Has a casting vote in case of tie.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vice-President → Ex-Officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha → Casting Vote

96. Vice-President Acting as President

Vice-President acts as President when:

  • Presidential office is vacant.

President is unable to discharge functions due to:

  • Illness.
  • Absence.
  • Death.
  • Resignation.
  • Removal.

During this period:

  • Vice-President exercises Presidential powers.
  • Enjoys Presidential privileges and immunities.
  • Does not perform Rajya Sabha Chairman's duties.

97. Vice-Presidential Salary

  • Vice-President receives salary and allowances as Chairman of Rajya Sabha.
  • No separate salary is attached merely to the office of Vice-President in the framework described by the notes.
  • While acting as President, Presidential salary and allowances apply.

98. Vice-Presidential Vacancy and Election Disputes

  • Vacancy election is held as soon as possible.
  • Newly elected Vice-President gets a full five-year term.
  • Election disputes are decided by Supreme Court under Article 71.
  • Supreme Court's decision is final and binding.

99. Prime Minister — Constitutional Position

  • Prime Minister is the real executive and principal political authority in India's parliamentary system.
  • President → Head of State.
  • Prime Minister → Head of Government.

Constitutional basis primarily includes:

  • Article 74.
  • Article 75.
  • Article 78.
📌 Must-Memorise

PM → Real Executive + Head of Government

100. Appointment of Prime Minister

  • President normally appoints leader of majority party or coalition in Lok Sabha.

In a hung House:

  • President selects person most likely to command confidence.
  • Majority must be demonstrated on floor of Lok Sabha.

101. Qualification and Six-Month Rule

  • Constitution prescribes no separate special qualification exclusively for Prime Minister in the notes.
  • Prime Minister must be qualified for membership of either House.
  • A non-MP may be appointed Prime Minister.
  • Such person must become a member of either House within six months or cease to hold office.
📌 Must-Memorise

Non-MP PM → Must Become MP within 6 Months

102. Oath and Tenure of Prime Minister

Prime Minister takes:

  • Oath of Office.
  • Oath of Secrecy.
  • Oaths are administered by President.
  • Prime Minister has no fixed constitutional tenure.
  • Continues in office while enjoying Lok Sabha confidence.

103. Central Position of Prime Minister

Prime Minister is:

  • Head of Government.
  • Leader of Council of Ministers.
  • Leader of Lok Sabha when a Lok Sabha member.
  • Principal adviser to President.
  • Chief policy maker.
  • Chief coordinator of administration.

104. Powers over Ministers

Prime Minister:

  • Recommends appointment of Ministers.
  • Allocates portfolios.
  • Reshuffles ministries.
  • Recommends dismissal.
  • Presides over Cabinet.
  • Coordinates departments.
  • Resolves ministerial differences.

105. Article 78 — Duties towards President

Prime Minister must:

  • Keep President informed.
  • Furnish information sought by President.
  • Place before Council any matter decided by an individual Minister when President so requires.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 78 → PM's Duties towards President

106. Prime Minister in Parliament

Prime Minister:

  • Guides Government business.
  • Introduces major policies.
  • Defends Government decisions.
  • Coordinates legislative agenda.
  • Advises on summoning and dissolution of Lok Sabha.

107. National and International Leadership

Prime Minister:

  • Leads national governance.
  • Represents India at multilateral summits.
  • Conducts bilateral engagement.
  • Shapes major national policy.

108. Important Bodies Chaired by Prime Minister

The notes identify the Prime Minister as Chairperson of bodies such as:

  • Union Cabinet.
  • NITI Aayog Governing Council.
  • Cabinet Committee on Security.
  • Other Cabinet Committees constituted by Government.

109. Descriptions of Prime Minister

Common constitutional-political descriptions include:

  • Keystone of the Cabinet Arch.
  • First among Equals.
  • Primus inter pares.
  • Effective parliamentary government depends heavily on Prime Ministerial leadership and majority support.

110. Council of Ministers — Constitutional Position

  • Council of Ministers is the real collective executive.

Constitutional basis:

  • Articles 74 and 75.
  • There shall be a Council of Ministers with Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise President.

111. Composition of Council of Ministers

It may include:

  • Prime Minister.
  • Cabinet Ministers.
  • Ministers of State.
  • Deputy Ministers, where appointed.

112. Appointment and Portfolios

  • President appoints Ministers on advice of Prime Minister.

Prime Minister determines:

  • Membership.
  • Portfolios.
  • Reshuffles.
  • Removal recommendations.

113. Oath and Membership of Ministers

Ministers take:

  • Oath of Office.
  • Oath of Secrecy.
  • A non-MP Minister must become a member of either House within six months or cease to hold office.

114. Categories of Ministers

The Constitution itself does not formally classify Ministers into these categories; they developed through practice.

Cabinet Ministers:

  • Senior Ministers.
  • Head major Ministries.
  • Participate in Cabinet decisions.

Ministers of State — Independent Charge:

  • Head Ministries independently.
  • May attend Cabinet when invited.

Ministers of State — Attached:

  • Assist Cabinet Ministers.

Deputy Ministers:

  • Assist senior Ministers.
  • Do not independently head Ministries.
  • Rarely appointed at Union level.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Minister Categories → Parliamentary Practice

Not Express Constitutional Classification

115. Maximum Size of Union Ministry

Total number of Ministers, including Prime Minister, cannot exceed:

  • 15% of Lok Sabha strength.

Limit was introduced by:

  • 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003.

Objectives included:

  • Prevent oversized ministries.
  • Reduce patronage.
  • Improve efficiency.
📌 Must-Memorise

91st Amendment → Union Ministry ≤ 15% of Lok Sabha

116. Council of Ministers vs Cabinet

Council of Ministers:

  • Constitutional body.
  • Includes all categories of Ministers.
  • Larger body.
  • Articles 74 and 75.

Cabinet:

  • Smaller inner body.
  • Mainly senior Cabinet Ministers.
  • Principal policy-making core.
  • Specifically recognised in Article 352.
📌 Must-Memorise

Council → Larger

Cabinet → Inner Core

117. Functions of Council of Ministers

Functions include:

  • Policy formulation.
  • Administration.
  • Legislation.
  • Budget preparation.
  • Foreign affairs.
  • Defence.
  • Internal security.
  • Economic planning.
  • Implementation of laws.
  • Inter-ministerial coordination.

118. Responsibility to Parliament

Ministers:

  • Participate in debates.
  • Answer parliamentary questions.
  • Pilot Government Bills.
  • Defend Government policies.
  • Remain collectively responsible to Lok Sabha.

119. Advice to President

Council of Ministers advises President regarding matters such as:

  • Appointments.
  • Dissolution of Lok Sabha.
  • Ordinances.
  • Emergency proclamations.
  • Executive decisions.

120. Cabinet System

  • India adopted the Westminster Cabinet model from the United Kingdom with constitutional adaptations.

Real political authority is exercised by:

  • Prime Minister.
  • Cabinet.
  • Cabinet is the central policy-making core of the Union Executive.

121. Constitutional Recognition of Cabinet

  • Articles 74 and 75 refer primarily to Council of Ministers.
  • The word Cabinet received express constitutional recognition in Article 352 through the 44th Amendment for National Emergency purposes.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

“Cabinet” Explicitly Mentioned → Article 352

122. Major Cabinet Functions

Cabinet:

  • Frames national policy.
  • Takes major administrative decisions.
  • Approves important Bills.
  • Prepares Budget.
  • Coordinates Ministries.
  • Advises President.
  • Decides defence and national-security matters.
  • Approves international agreements.
  • Manages crises and emergencies.

123. Cabinet Meetings

  • Cabinet meetings are chaired by Prime Minister.

They deal with:

  • National policy.
  • Legislation.
  • Economy.
  • Security.
  • Inter-ministerial coordination.
  • Decisions bind all Ministers under collective responsibility.

124. Cabinet Secretariat

Cabinet Secretariat:

  • Is headed by Cabinet Secretary.
  • Coordinates inter-ministerial work.
  • Prepares agenda.
  • Records decisions.
  • Monitors implementation.
  • Facilitates communication.
  • The attached notes describe Cabinet Secretary as the senior-most civil servant in Government of India.

125. Cabinet Committees

Cabinet Committees:

  • Reduce Cabinet workload.
  • Improve speed.
  • Improve coordination.
  • Allow specialised consideration.

They may be:

  • Standing Committees.
  • Ad hoc Committees.

126. Major Cabinet Committees

Important examples listed in the notes include:

Cabinet Committee on Security — CCS:

  • National security.
  • Defence policy.
  • Strategic and nuclear affairs.
  • Internal security.

Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs — CCEA:

  • Economic policy.
  • Investment.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Major economic decisions.

Cabinet Committee on Political Affairs — CCPA:

  • Political affairs.

Parliamentary Affairs Committee:

  • Government–Parliament coordination.

Appointments Committee:

  • Senior civil servants.
  • Heads of institutions.

Accommodation Committee:

  • Government accommodation matters.

127. Prime Minister and Cabinet Committees

  • Prime Minister chairs the Cabinet Committee on Security.
  • Number and composition of Cabinet Committees may change through Government decisions.

128. Article 75(3)

  • Article 75(3) declares that Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to House of the People.
  • The Council functions as one united constitutional body.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 75(3) → Collective Responsibility to Lok Sabha

129. Meaning of Collective Responsibility

Collective responsibility means joint responsibility for:

  • Government policy.
  • Cabinet decisions.
  • Administrative action.
  • Legislation.
  • Ministers must publicly support final Cabinet decisions even where internal disagreement existed.

130. Effect of No-Confidence Motion

  • Government survives only while it retains Lok Sabha majority.

If Council loses a no-confidence vote:

  • Prime Minister and entire Council of Ministers must resign.
  • Majority doubts should be resolved through a floor test.

131. Cabinet Solidarity and Secrecy

  • Ministers may debate freely within Cabinet.

Once decision is taken:

  • All Ministers must publicly defend it.
  • A Minister unable to support the decision should resign.
  • Cabinet discussions remain confidential under Oath of Secrecy.

132. Individual Responsibility

Individual Minister:

  • Answers for own Ministry.
  • Must explain departmental decisions in Parliament.
  • May resign.
  • May be removed when Prime Minister advises President.

133. Article 75(2) — Pleasure of President

  • Ministers hold office during pleasure of President.

In parliamentary practice described by the notes:

  • This pleasure operates through Prime Minister's advice.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 75(2) → Ministers Hold Office during President's Pleasure

134. Collective vs Individual Responsibility

Collective:

  • Entire Council responsible together.
  • Article 75(3).
  • Loss of confidence removes entire Council.
  • Responsibility to Lok Sabha.

Individual:

  • Minister responsible for own department.
  • Connected with Article 75(2) and parliamentary convention.
  • One Minister may resign or be removed.
  • Responsibility to Prime Minister and Parliament.

135. Legal Responsibility and Article 77

  • Constitution does not expressly impose personal legal responsibility on Ministers for official Presidential acts in the manner described by the notes.
  • Union executive action is authenticated under Article 77.

136. Coalition and Minority Governments

Collective responsibility continues regardless of whether Government is:

  • Single-party.
  • Coalition.
  • Minority Government.
  • All Ministers must support officially approved Government policy.

137. Attorney General — Constitutional Office

Attorney General of India is:

  • Highest law officer of India.
  • Principal legal adviser to Union Government.

Constitutional basis:

  • Article 76.
  • President appoints Attorney General.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 76 → Attorney General of India

138. Qualifications of Attorney General

The appointee must be qualified to become a Supreme Court judge.

Qualifications mentioned include:

  • Citizen of India.
  • High Court judge for at least five years, or
  • High Court advocate for at least ten years, or
  • Distinguished jurist in President's opinion.

139. Tenure and Remuneration of Attorney General

  • No fixed constitutional term.
  • Holds office during President's pleasure.
  • No prescribed retirement age.
  • Remuneration is determined by President.

140. Functions of Attorney General

Attorney General:

  • Advises Government of India on legal matters.
  • Gives opinions referred by President.
  • Appears for Union before Supreme Court.
  • Represents Union in High Courts where required.
  • Performs legal duties assigned by President.
  • Discharges constitutional and statutory functions.

141. Right of Audience

  • Attorney General has right of audience in all courts in India.

This includes:

  • Supreme Court.
  • High Courts.
  • Other courts as required.
📌 Must-Memorise

Attorney General → Right of Audience in All Courts in India

142. Parliamentary Rights of Attorney General

Attorney General may:

  • Speak in either House.
  • Participate in parliamentary proceedings.
  • Participate in committees where named.

But:

  • Has no right to vote.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Attorney General → Can Speak, Cannot Vote

143. Private Practice

  • Attorney General is not a full-time Government employee according to the attached notes.
  • May engage in private legal practice subject to conflict-of-interest conventions.

Ordinarily:

  • Does not advise against Government of India.
  • Does not appear against Union Government.
  • Avoids briefs conflicting with official duties.

144. Attorney General vs Solicitor General

Attorney General:

  • Constitutional office.
  • Article 76.
  • Highest Union law officer.

Solicitor General:

  • Not a constitutional office.
  • Government appointment.
  • Assists Attorney General.

Additional Solicitors General:

  • Also non-constitutional appointments.

149. Seventh Constitutional Amendment, 1956

The notes associate the Seventh Amendment with consequential executive changes following:

  • State reorganisation.
  • Union Territory administration.

  • President must assent to a duly passed Constitutional Amendment Bill.

  • Emergencies

  • Anti-defection provisions were introduced.

  • Applicable disqualification period ends.

What is difference between Council of Ministers and Cabinet? → Council includes all Ministers; Cabinet is the smaller senior policy-making core.

Where is the word Cabinet explicitly constitutionally recognised according to the notes? → Article 352.

Who heads Cabinet Secretariat? → Cabinet Secretary.

How is Cabinet Secretary described in the notes? → Senior-most civil servant in Government of India.

Name major Cabinet Committees identified in the source. → CCS, CCEA, CCPA, Parliamentary Affairs, Appointments Committee and Accommodation Committee.

Who chairs Cabinet Committee on Security? → Prime Minister.

What is collective responsibility? → Entire Council stands or falls together and remains responsible to Lok Sabha.

What happens after loss of Lok Sabha confidence? → Prime Minister and entire Council must resign.

What is Cabinet solidarity? → Ministers must publicly support Cabinet decisions or resign.

Which Article relates to Ministers holding office during President's pleasure? → Article 75(2).

How does Presidential pleasure operate in practice? → Through Prime Minister's advice.

Which Article establishes Attorney General? → Article 76.

Who appoints Attorney General? → President.

Who is India's highest law officer? → Attorney General.

What qualifications must Attorney General possess? → Qualifications required for appointment as Supreme Court judge.

Does Attorney General have fixed constitutional tenure? → No.

Does Attorney General have a prescribed retirement age? → No.

Does Attorney General have right of audience in all courts in India? → Yes.

Can Attorney General speak in Parliament? → Yes.

Can Attorney General vote in Parliament? → No.

Is Solicitor General a constitutional office? → No.

Which Amendment made President constitutionally bound by ministerial advice? → 42nd Amendment, 1976.

Which Amendment allowed President to return advice once? → 44th Amendment, 1978.

Which Amendment limited size of Union Ministry? → 91st Amendment, 2003.

Which case held Council of Ministers continues after dissolution of Lok Sabha? → U.N.R. Rao v. Indira Gandhi, 1971.

Which leading case affirmed that President ordinarily acts on ministerial advice? → Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab, 1974.

Which case dealt with constitutional limits on executive discretion in 2006? → Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India.

Which 2016 case emphasised that constitutional discretion cannot replace constitutional procedure? → Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker.
